runs.text: Deixar a agoa de ſoar, ou

lines.note: Niyeiri describes boiling water ceasing to sound, rather than simply ceasing to boil. The Japanese principal parts and Portuguese ſoar agree with the following reference to noise.
This completes the noise made by boiling: the scope of Deixar above includes making a din. The tilde in cõ is kept as an abbreviation, not expanded.
Niyeyu is water that is boiling. Its yu element is part of the upright headword; agoa retains the source's spelling.
Niyetaguiri means boiling vigorously. The guiri spelling and the printed inflectional u are retained; fer- continues the Portuguese verb below.
This completes fer-/uer and explains the vigorous boiling as bubbling. The historical burbulhoẽs and its tilde on e are preserved.
This Niyoi is the verb glossed 'to groan.' Both principal-part marks are circumflexes; the spelling is not adjusted to a different modern verb from the sound alone.

runs.text: Particula que junta com outras pala-

lines.note: Niyotte is described as a connective particle used with other words. The physical pala- ending belongs to palauras, not the Japanese entry.

runs.text: uras quer dizer porque, ou por quanto.

lines.note: The particle's function is explained as 'because' or 'inasmuch as.' This ends the NI material before the separate NO section heading.

Nô denotes arts, accomplishments, or abilities. The enlarged N omitted by OCR is restored and marked as a two-line initial; the taller crop includes the whole letter. The second sense begins with Itẽ.
The second sense is a dramatic performance, with Nôuo ſuru meaning to perform it. This indented line stands beside the large initial; re- continues Portuguese repreſentar below.
This completes 'perform a play or tragedy.' The theatrical gloss belongs to Nô and is not the grammatical particle No that follows.
The unaccented particle No is assigned genitive and nominative functions in the dictionary's own grammatical description. The capitalized case names and historical u spellings remain literal.

runs.text: Particula de chamar por alguem. i, Oulà.

lines.note: This marked Nǒ is a particle used to call someone, compared with Portuguese Oulà. The caron distinguishes it graphically from the earlier circumflexed Nô.
The next homograph means brains or marrow-like contents, glossed Miolos. Its caron is retained rather than changed to the previous Nô's circumflex.
This No is the shaft of an arrow. The dictionary's frecha spelling is preserved without inserting a modern Japanese identification into the canonical text.
No means a field, and Noni naru introduces a figurative 'become a field' expression. Both visible paragraph marks are retained, including the one before Per met.

runs.text: Estar tudo deſtruido, ou deſpouoado como cãpo.

lines.note: The figurative sense is being wholly destroyed or depopulated like an open field. The nasal abbreviation in cãpo and the printed st form in Estar are retained.
Noaſobi denotes recreation in the countryside. The repeated example starts with the same word divided at Noaſo- across the physical line.
Noaſobini zzuru means going out into the fields for recreation. The doubled zz is visible and retained; the Portuguese word gap after Sair corrects the OCR's joined Sairao.
Nobara is an open field with grass. The printed definition is not silently replaced with a different modern homograph or botanical sense.
Nobaxi is transitive extending or lengthening. Its principal part aita is the historical printed form, and the definition continues with examples rather than another headword.
Qiuo nobaſu is introduced as figurative relief or relaxation of the spirit. The clearly printed paragraph mark missing from OCR is restored; Deſaba- continues into far below.

The Portuguese completes Deſaba-/far, to relieve or expand the heart; the initial f is not long s. Only one tilde is visible, over a in coração, correcting coraçãõ. The example's short s in nobasǒ is retained.

The example describes going up to a cool place to relax. The damaged citation reads Mon rather than OCR Mor; no terminal point is supplied where none is clearly visible. The Portuguese translation begins Subio ao on this same line.

runs.text: lugar freſco da viração pera eſparecer. ¶

lines.note: The translation mentions a cool, breezy place for recreation. The historical eſparecer is retained, and Fi- starts the next upright Japanese example.
Fitouo nobaſu is followed by Latin 'but better' and a preferred Japanese expression. The weak surviving e supports Sed, not the OCR gap S d; no hyphen is supplied after the printed line-final ſu.

runs.text: Fazer eſcapar, ou fugir a alguem.

lines.note: This completes Tenobaxini ſu-/ru and explains allowing or causing someone to escape. The line remains a continuation of the Nobaxi entry.
This noun Nobe means a field. It is distinct from the inflecting verb Nobe on the next physical line.
The verb Nobe means extending or prolonging. Its listed forms remain uru and eta; the examples follow on separate lines.
Danguiuo noburu is glossed as preaching. The final Iy, with a capital I rather than OCR lowercase l, begins the separate expression continued by noburu below; the grave in Prègar is retained.

runs.text: Dilatar com palauras, ou fazer cõ

lines.note: Iy noburu is explained as prolonging something with words or persuading someone to wait. The abbreviated cõ leads into the object alguem on the next line.
This completes the explanatory clause, making someone wait longer. It belongs to the verbal entry above and is not a separate definition.
Nobecu denotes delay or the devices and excuses used to defer action. The source's eſcuſas is retained as printed.
The delay concerns carrying out something. The tilde is on u in dalgũa, and Nobe- begins the repeated headword in the following example.

runs.text: Dilatar dedia em dia com eſcuſas,

lines.note: Nobecuuo yù is glossed as delaying from day to day with excuses. The aligned OCR's grave in yù and close dedia are retained; the damaged accent is not automatically replaced by a caron on lexical grounds.
Achaques adds pretexts or excuses to the preceding explanation. The ampersand and abbreviation close this entry.
Nobetçuqe means attaching something while spreading or extending it. The printed Estendendo retains its locally aligned st form; the compound headword is not split.
The example concerns spreading and attaching metal closely to a surface. The scan's separation nobe tçuqetaga is kept even though the headword is printed as one compound.
The upright Xid. is a citation label, followed by the translation about spreading and attaching metal or sheets. It is marked as a citation for optional whole-word typeface review.
This specifies iron sheets and closes the metal-working example. There is no additional Japanese material on the short continuation.

runs.text: Fogo que ſe poem aos campos pera quei-

lines.note: This Nobi is fire set to fields. Its damaged initial is N, not OCR X; quei- begins Portuguese quei-/mar below.
The field fire burns dry grass. This completes the literal definition without adding a modern purpose or agricultural explanation.
This Nobi denotes stretching oneself, with Nobiuo ſuru as the example. The historical i in eſpriguiçarſe is preserved rather than modernized.
The verb Nobi is intransitive lengthening. The example Figa nobi- concerns a day being extended or deferred; the damaged n is retained from its surviving stroke.

runs.text: Dilatouſe, ou diferioſe o dia determina

lines.note: The example means that an appointed day was extended or deferred. The scan supports diferioſe, not difenoſe, and the worn m in determina corrects deternina. The word continues with do at the top of column 2 without a supplied hyphen.
The initial do completes determina-/do across the column boundary. A new example, Inochiga nobita, then applies lengthening to a person's life; the tilde remains on u in algũa.

runs.text: Dilatarſe a vida do que estaua pera morrer.

lines.note: The example means prolonging the life of someone who was about to die. The printed estaua spelling and its locally aligned short s are retained.

Xei and taqe offer alternative ways of expressing stature in the example. The Portuguese describes becoming tall, with de leading into corpo below; no Japanese term here is embedded in the Portuguese run.
This completes growing tall in body or growing considerably. Crecer is kept in its historical spelling rather than supplied with an extra s.
Nobiagari means rising while stretching or straightening oneself. The visibly printed final point after aleuantarſe, omitted by OCR, is restored.
The quoted example says that the named subject Xǒzon is not at all perturbed and rises forcefully. The caron in Xǒzon and the historical idaqeda- spelling remain as printed.

This completes idaqeda-/cani and the quotation, followed by the upright citation Toſ. The name at the start of the Portuguese translation has a caron, not OCR õ; its upright capital X and italic remainder are preserved as the visible mixed setting.

runs.text: ſem ſe perturbar ſe aleuantou de joelhos muito

lines.note: The translation describes rising on the knees without disturbance. On the second pass, the damaged oval after j is read as o in joelhos rather than OCR c; its thin right contour is weak, so the choice remains a nonblocking caveat rather than a claimed clear impression.
The person rises very erect and speaks as follows. The two long s characters in diſſe and the distinct ß-shaped sort in aßi are preserved rather than made uniform.

Nobiru denotes wild garlic. A second-pass comparison with Alhos in f366 c1-l040 and the italic h in hum and homens identifies the b-like loop as this font's h; Alhos therefore corrects OCR Albos rather than preserving a spurious printed anomaly.

runs.text: Bandeiras que leuão os ſoldados na

lines.note: This Nobori means the banners carried by soldiers. The nasal spelling leuão and the long s in ſoldados are retained.
This completes 'in war' in the banner definition. It is a short continuation, not a separate headword.
This noun Nobori means an ascent, distinct from the banner homograph and the verb in the next line.
The verb Nobori means ascending. Its first example, Curaini no-/boru, applies the idea to rising in rank or dignity.
The first example is translated as rising in dignity. Miyaco- begins a second example about going to the capital, with its directional particle on the next line.
Miyacoye noboru means going to the capital. The second Miyaco occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is italic there; it is marked for optional whole-word typeface review.

Noboricoye means climbing over something. The damaged vowel after N has a rounded trace, supporting o rather than OCR e; the lexical match is also confirmed by the supplied NINJAL entry, without normalizing other letters.
The Portuguese completes 'pass over by climbing.' The example begins by putting a hand on a wall or enclosure; paßar preserves its ß-shaped sort.
The example continues with an attempt to climb over together. The circumflex in dôjini and the printed separation nobori coyento are retained, regardless of the compound headword spelling.

The quotation ends with upright &c. and the upright citation Taif.; Lib. 3. and the translation are italic. The translation begins by putting a hand on the wall, so no OCR point is retained after the line-final à.

runs.text: parede da cerca fizerão por ſubir, & paßar to-

lines.note: They attempt to climb and cross the enclosure wall. The scan shows r and a nasal mark in fizerão, correcting fizenão; to- continues todos below.
This completes 'all at once,' translating the simultaneous action of the example. The nasal abbreviation hũa remains unexpanded.
Noboricudari combines ascent and descent. The repeated example begins with the round vowel No-, not OCR Nu-; decer is preserved in its printed spelling.
This completes the example Nobori cudariuo ſuru, to go up and down. Its internal word separation is retained rather than joined to match the headword.
Noborifaxi is a ladder or stair for ascending. The f belongs to the historical spelling of faxi and is distinct from the long s in Noboriſaxi below.
Noboriſaca is an ascending slope. The source separates a cima, and the long s in the headword is preserved.
Noboriſaxi denotes men carrying banners. The nasal marks in Homẽs, leuão, and hũas are preserved individually; the headword's ſ is not the f of the ladder entry.

runs.text: altas pegadas em bambus na guerra.

lines.note: The banners are tall and attached to bamboo in wartime. This explains the carriers' equipment without introducing another headword.
Noboritçudoi describes many people assembling or going upward together. Both principal parts carry circumflexes; gẽ continues gente below without an invented hyphen.
This completes the group proceeding together to a high place. The initial te is the continuation of gẽ, not a separate word in the continuous sense.
Noboritçuqi means arriving by ascending. The visible initial N corrects OCR X, and Portuguese Subindo corrects Cubindo; the historical uita principal part is retained.

runs.text: Bambu em que vai pegada a bã-

lines.note: Noborizauo is a bamboo flagpole. The scan supports em and joined pegada, correcting ent and pega da; the line-final nasalized syllable is bã-, with a rather than OCR u beneath the tilde.
This completes bã-/deira de campo, the field banner carried on the pole. The source's abbreviated syllable is not expanded into an inserted n.
Noboxe means making someone ascend or sending them upward. The comma visible after eta is restored; ſuru and the alternate oita remain the printed forms, without grammatical normalization.
The destination is the capital, Miyaco, here embedded in italic Portuguese. The example starts with selected or capable soldiers; the original Cucqiǒno spelling and caron are preserved.
The Japanese specifies assembling seventy-four men and sending them up as attackers. Its exact numeral is retained even though the following Portuguese paraphrases it as more than seventy.

runs.text: Ajuntando mais de ſetenta ſoldados esco-

lines.note: The upright citation Xid. is followed by the translation about gathering more than seventy selected soldiers. The physical esco- ending and its locally aligned short s are retained.

runs.text: lhidos mandou os ao Miyaco por matadores.

lines.note: The translation completes 'selected' and says they were sent to Miyaco as killers. Miyaco is italic within Portuguese, and the printed separation mandou os is not modernized with a hyphen.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de entrar a frecha

lines.note: Nobucani is labeled an adverb and describes an arrow penetrating deeply. The explanatory Adu. remains italic with the Portuguese rather than being treated as a citation.
The definition specifies deep entry into the body, followed by an example of an arrow sticking deeply. The Japanese remains an upright standalone example, not an embedded typeface term.

runs.text: Pregarſe a frecha muito dentro do corpo.

lines.note: This translates the example as the arrow lodging far inside the body. The long s in Pregarſe and historical frecha are retained.

runs.text: Eſcaramuça, ou encontro que ſe tem

lines.note: Nobuxi is a skirmish or preliminary encounter. The weak middle m of Eſcaramuça is restored from surviving strokes and comparison with its clear repetition below, correcting the broken OCR Eſcaran uça.
The encounter occurs before the main battle. Nobuxiuo caquru is then given as the example, separated by the visible paragraph mark.
The example means engaging in that preliminary encounter or skirmish. This clear eſcaramuça also helps identify the worn word two lines above.

runs.text: Gente, que vai diante pera eſ-

lines.note: Nobuxino xu names the people going ahead for the skirmish. The damaged rounded vowel supports No-, not OCR Nu-; the line ends eſ-, without the extra OCR a before the hyphen.
This completes eſ-/ta and specifies the skirmish. The vowel in eſcaramuça is u, correcting the OCR t without altering the historical word.

Nochi means 'after,' as in after a battle or war. The headword's o and the final s of Depois correct Nuchi and Depoiu. The italic De- continues on the next page; the separate italic pois below is the catchword, not part of this body line.
